title: Unaligned checkpoints: save the waiting records too
goal: See why a recovery snapshot sometimes needs the queue as well as the running total.
concept:
A cashier has counted $10. Two receipts, worth $2 and $3, are waiting on the desk. A useful handover must account for both the counted money and the waiting receipts.

A streaming operator has the same problem. Its saved state might contain a running total, while records still sit in network buffers. A checkpoint is a coordinated recovery snapshot. In an aligned checkpoint, inputs wait at checkpoint markers until the operator has a consistent boundary. Backpressure can make this wait long.

An unaligned checkpoint records in-flight data as well as operator state. Checkpoint markers can overtake buffered records. Recovery restores the saved state and processes the saved records. This trades less waiting on busy channels for more checkpoint data.
example:
Our snapshot stores state=10 and channel=[2,3]. After a crash, replaying that channel produces 15. Saving only 10 loses the waiting records in this deliberately broken recovery model. Saving 15 and replaying the same two records would count them twice. The snapshot must describe a consistent cut through the work.

Flink coordinates that cut across operators and channels. This example isolates the accounting; it does not implement the distributed protocol.

use_case.when: Checkpoint alignment and start delays grow during backpressure, while checkpoint storage still has capacity.
use_case.example: A Kafka-to-Flink aggregation spends most checkpoint time waiting behind queued records. Compare aligned and unaligned runs with the same workload; inspect duration, checkpoint bytes, and recovery time.
use_case.decision: Consider unaligned checkpoints when waiting dominates. If object-store throughput is already the bottleneck, extra channel data can make things worse. Locate the delay before changing the setting.

practice: Predict what survives a crash. Save, crash, restore, then replay one record per click. Compare saving the queue with draining it first. Both should reach the same total. Finally try the deliberately broken state-only snapshot.
boundary: JavaScript executes local arithmetic on one synthetic channel. It omits barrier coordination, source positions, sink transactions, storage latency, and rescaling. A real unaligned checkpoint still takes time and may wait for the current record to finish.
sim: Compare two valid cuts: save the waiting records, or finish them before saving. The broken option does neither; it is not an aligned checkpoint.
questions: The replay saves 10 and [2,3]. What should recovery produce?
Replaying the two not-yet-counted records adds 5, once.
Why can an unaligned checkpoint help?
It saves in-flight data instead of waiting for it to drain
The records remain part of recovery. This does not add sink transactions.
When is this a poor first fix?
Extra saved channel data can worsen an I/O bottleneck.
written_questions: Which metrics distinguish barrier waiting from slow checkpoint storage?
What error results from saving state 15 and replaying [2,3] again?
sources: Living documentation; stable version 2.3.0; unaligned checkpoints introduced in 1.11

steps.note: Two records have not contributed to the total.
Save both parts of the recovery snapshot.
Simulate losing process memory. The durable snapshot survives.
Including the saved channel gives 15; ignoring it leaves 10.

walkthrough.limit: Executed Python accounting, not Flink. The lab uses repeated +2 records so you can vary queue length.

visual_explanation: The dashed worker area is temporary memory. The solid snapshot area survives a crash. With two +2 records, the unaligned-style snapshot holds total 10 plus two waiting records; recovery replays them to reach 14. The aligned-style toy drains those records before saving, so the snapshot holds total 14 and an empty channel. Both account for every record exactly once. The deliberately broken option holds 10 and no channel, losing 4. It is NOT an aligned checkpoint. This is single-channel accounting, not Flink barrier coordination.

product_sections.title: Databricks: checkpoint identity and Delta retries
product_sections.html:
Use case. A receipt-copy job stops after writing a batch. You need to restart without copying those rows twice. Use a durable checkpoint for the same Structured Streaming query and a Delta sink. This example copies rows; the total is queried afterward, so it needs no aggregation state store.

Think of two durable records: the checkpoint remembers the query’s progress; the Delta transaction log remembers a batch already accepted by that query. If progress recording trails the sink commit, a retry can recognize that accepted batch. Replacing the checkpoint starts a new query identity and can copy old input again.

Different from Flink: this is micro-batch replay and sink deduplication. It does not enable Flink’s unaligned-checkpoint feature or save Flink network buffers.

Why can the same batch return without adding rows?

Predict the copied total after restart. Then switch to a new checkpoint and try again.

1  read pending receipts into batch A:12  Delta accepts A:1 and saves rows3  crash before checkpoint records completion4  restart; check query + batch identity5  record successful progress

Boundary. The browser executes a simplified JavaScript model of query identity, batch identity, and durable output. It does not run Spark or reproduce checkpoint files. The snippets below were checked against documentation but were not executed in a Databricks account. Expected results are predictions. Source retention, supported restart changes, and sink choice still matter; arbitrary external API calls are outside Delta’s protection.

Run in Databricks · within the 9-minute block when a sandbox is available

Use a fresh sandbox schema for setup; create the writable volume beforehand. SQL is the setup and inspection language. Python expresses the streaming writer. Run once before inserting r2/r3, then rerun after that insert. Rerun a third time without new input: expect 15 again. Do not delete a production checkpoint to test the failure.

-- Run in an existing, authorized sandbox catalog/schema.
CREATE TABLE sandbox.study17.receipts (id STRING, amount INT) USING DELTA;
INSERT INTO sandbox.study17.receipts VALUES ('base', 10);
-- Run the Python stream once. Then add the next receipts:
INSERT INTO sandbox.study17.receipts VALUES ('r2', 2), ('r3', 3);
-- Run the SAME Python stream again, using the SAME checkpoint.
SELECT SUM(amount) FROM sandbox.study17.receipts_copy; -- expected: 15
# Prerequisite: sandbox.study17.checkpoints is a writable UC volume.
# Use a dedicated path per query. Keep this path on subsequent runs.
q = (spark.readStream.table("sandbox.study17.receipts")
     .writeStream
     .format("delta")
     .option("checkpointLocation",
             "/Volumes/sandbox/study17/checkpoints/receipts_copy")
     .trigger(availableNow=True)
     .toTable("sandbox.study17.receipts_copy"))
q.awaitTermination()
  1. Run CREATE TABLE and the base=10 INSERT only.
  2. Run the Python cell: the target receives 10.
  3. Insert r2=2 and r3=3 into the source.
  4. Run the same Python cell, then query the target total: expect 15.
  5. Run that Python cell once more with no new source data: expect 15 again.

If you cannot access a sandbox today, complete the model and mark product execution not run. A browser simulation is not hands-on Databricks experience.

product_sections.title: Snowflake: a stream advances when the work commits
product_sections.html:
Use case. New receipts land in a Snowflake table. A SQL job copies only the new inserts into a downstream table. An append-only stream identifies the new rows. Its stored position is tied to table history; it is not a queue containing copies of the rows.

Reading the stream with SELECT leaves its position unchanged. A committed transaction that consumes it with INSERT advances the position. Rollback keeps both the old target data and the old position, so the next attempt can read the same change set.

Different from Flink: this is transactional change consumption inside Snowflake. There is no unaligned-checkpoint switch for a Snowflake stream.

Which changes cross the COMMIT boundary?

Watch the durable total and stream position together. The dashed box is tentative work.

1  SELECT * FROM changes;2  BEGIN; INSERT INTO copy SELECT ... FROM changes;3  ROLLBACK; -- or COMMIT4  BEGIN; INSERT ... SELECT ...; COMMIT;

Boundary. This JavaScript model has two inserts, one consumer, no concurrent writers, and enough retained source history. V0/V1 are illustrative table versions, not literal Snowflake offset values. Real streams can become stale if history expires. A task can schedule the SQL, but scheduling alone does not establish this transaction boundary. The Snowflake SQL has not been executed in an account here.

Run in Snowflake · within the 9-minute block when a sandbox is available

These are persistent teaching objects; use a dedicated sandbox schema. Use a sandbox role with permission to create tables and streams, plus an active warehouse. Drop the three study17 objects after inspecting the results. Inspect the result after ROLLBACK before continuing.

-- Use an authorized sandbox schema and an active small warehouse.
CREATE TABLE study17_receipts (id STRING, amount INTEGER);
INSERT INTO study17_receipts VALUES ('base', 10);
CREATE TABLE study17_copy AS SELECT * FROM study17_receipts;
CREATE STREAM study17_changes
  ON TABLE study17_receipts APPEND_ONLY = TRUE;
INSERT INTO study17_receipts VALUES ('r2', 2), ('r3', 3);

SELECT * FROM study17_changes; -- inspect; position does not advance
BEGIN TRANSACTION;
INSERT INTO study17_copy SELECT id, amount FROM study17_changes;
ROLLBACK; -- rehearsal: neither target rows nor stream advance persist

BEGIN TRANSACTION;
INSERT INTO study17_copy SELECT id, amount FROM study17_changes;
COMMIT;
SELECT SUM(amount) FROM study17_copy; -- expected: 15
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM study17_changes; -- expected: 0

After COMMIT, repeat the consuming INSERT in a new transaction: it adds no rows while the source is unchanged. This shows position advancement, not deduplication of independently inserted duplicate business events.

product_comparison.html:
SystemRecovery memoryWatch out for
Flink unalignedOperator state + in-flight channel dataMore snapshot bytes; not a cure for slow storage
DatabricksQuery checkpoint + Delta accepted-batch identityA new checkpoint creates a fresh query
SnowflakeStream position + committed target transactionSELECT does not consume; history must remain available

Choose by the workload you actually operate. Diagnose Flink barrier delay, preserve Databricks query identity, or use Snowflake transactional change consumption. These are related answers to “what has safely finished?”; their controls are not interchangeable.
product_comparison.markdown:
| System | Recovery memory | Boundary |
|---|---|---|
| Flink unaligned | State plus in-flight channel data | Snapshot size can rise |
| Databricks | Query checkpoint and Delta batch identity | Fresh checkpoint starts fresh query |
| Snowflake | Stream position and target transaction | SELECT does not consume; retained history required |

product_questions: After a Databricks Delta sink commit, restarting with the same valid checkpoint replays a batch. What protects the copied rows?
The same query/batch can be recognized by the Delta sink. A new query identity changes that boundary. This says nothing about independent duplicate business events.
You SELECT a Snowflake stream, then INSERT from it inside a transaction that rolls back. What persists?
SELECT does not consume the stream. The rolled-back consuming transaction preserves the old target and stream position, allowing a retry.

title: Bloom filters: a cheap no, a cautious maybe
goal: Avoid needless database reads without treating a probabilistic hint as an exact answer.
concept:
A receptionist keeps a short checklist of initials. If your initials are absent, your name is absent. If they are present, someone else might share them. The receptionist still needs the full guest list.

A Bloom filter is a compact set of bits. Adding an ID turns on positions chosen by hash functions. A lookup checks those positions: one zero means absent from the inserted set; all ones mean possibly present. Different IDs can share positions.
example:
Our eight-bit toy uses x % 8 and (3*x+1) % 8. Inserting 1 and 2 produces [0,1,1,0,1,0,0,1]. Query 9 finds two ones, although it was never inserted: a false positive. Query 3 checks positions 3 and 2. Position 3 is zero, so 3 is absent.

The safe read path is: a negative skips the expensive lookup; a positive goes to the authoritative database. A positive must never mean “discard this payment because it was already processed.”

use_case.when: Most lookups ask for nonexistent keys, and avoiding those reads saves substantial work.
use_case.example: A metadata service checks object IDs against a large catalog. A complete filter can reject absent IDs cheaply; possible matches still read the catalog.
use_case.decision: Control freshness and completeness. For exact deduplication use an authoritative unique key or transaction. For a small set, an ordinary hash set is simpler.

practice: Follow the two arrows from query 9 to bits 1 and 4. Who switched those bits on? Compare 9 with 1, then try 3. Turn on the broken shortcut to see where a false positive becomes a wrong answer.
boundary: The browser executes an eight-bit toy with deliberately weak, correlated hashes. It is not Redis or a false-positive-rate estimator. The no-false-negative property covers inserted items in an intact filter, not records absent from a stale filter.
questions: ID 9 checks two set bits. What should the service do?
Shared bits are not proof. Clearing them can damage other IDs.
Why may query 3 skip the exact read in this complete toy?
Every inserted ID sets both positions. One zero rules out membership in that inserted set.
A new catalog ID has not reached the filter. Is its negative safe for the catalog?
More hashes cannot repair a missing update.
written_questions: Why is this a read optimization rather than an exact processed-message marker?
How would you detect a filter built from an incomplete catalog snapshot?
sources: Living documentation; publication date not stated

steps.code:
var bits = new java.util.BitSet(8);
var inserted = java.util.Set.of(1, 2);
steps.note: Begin with zero bits and an exact reference set.

steps.code: for (int id : inserted) { bits.set(id % 8); bits.set((3 * id + 1) % 8); }
steps.note: Set positions 1, 4, 2, and 7.

steps.code:
int query = 9;
boolean maybe = bits.get(query % 8) && bits.get((3 * query + 1) % 8);
steps.note: ID 9 collides with ID 1.

steps.code:
boolean exact = inserted.contains(query);
boolean falsePositive = maybe && !exact;
steps.note: The exact lookup rejects 9. The filter did not corrupt the answer.

walkthrough.limit: Executed Java BitSet example with teaching hashes; no Redis or database process.

visual_explanation: The arrows connect the query’s two hash calculations to the exact bit positions they inspect. Labels below each set bit show which inserted ID set it. ID 9 and ID 1 point to the same two bits, even though only ID 1 is in the catalog. ID 3 points to bit 3, which is zero: that single zero stops the lookup. A MAYBE continues to the exact catalog unless the broken shortcut bypasses it.

title: Automation payback: include the work that remains
goal: Turn a recurring platform chore into an explicit build-versus-maintain decision.
concept:
You can wash dishes by hand or spend time installing a dishwasher. The machine saves repeated effort, but installation and upkeep still count. Automation has the same shape.

Toil is recurring operational work that leaves little lasting improvement. Measure one unit of work. Compare manual effort with residual human effort plus maintenance. A script that constantly breaks can move the work rather than remove it.
example:
For 20 standard access requests weekly, a self-service path reduces review from 15 to 3 minutes each. Weekly maintenance takes one hour. At week 4, manual handling has cost 20 hours. Automation has cost 24 build hours plus 8 operating hours: 32. At week 8 both total 40. At week 12, automation has saved 12 hours.

This original estimate is not a universal funding rule. Expose assumptions, assign an owner, and measure the result after launch.

use_case.when: Teams compete for capacity to automate recurring tickets, approvals, or platform operations.
use_case.example: Compare self-service Kafka topic provisioning with a manual request queue. Measure volume, review time, exceptions, and upkeep before promising saved engineering time.
use_case.decision: Check that expected useful lifetime and benefits justify the cost. Low-volume work may only need simplification. Reduced errors or faster customer response can justify investment even when hours alone do not.

practice: Predict which line will be lower at week 12. Lower requests to 5: the lines become parallel. Why does the 24-hour build cost never get repaid? Then raise upkeep to 6 and explain why the gap grows.
boundary: The browser calculates synthetic effort with constant demand and maintenance. It omits adoption, uncertainty, incidents, financial valuation, and risk reduction. This is a decision aid, not a funding algorithm.
questions: 24 build hours; 3 net hours saved weekly. When is effort equal?
24/3 = 8. Counting all 5 manual hours as savings ignores remaining work.
At 5 requests weekly and 1 upkeep hour, what is net saving?
Manual is 1.25 hours; residual review is 0.25 plus 1 upkeep.
Little hour savings, but fewer dangerous manual errors: what next?
Make other benefits explicit instead of changing the arithmetic.
written_questions: What would you measure before funding this project?
How would twice as much exception handling change the decision?

steps.note: List recurring work and initial investment.

steps.code:
manual_weekly = requests * manual_minutes / 60
auto_weekly = requests * residual_minutes / 60 + maintenance_hours
steps.note: Compare 5 hours with 2, not with zero.

steps.code:
net_saved = manual_weekly - auto_weekly
payback_weeks = build_hours / net_saved if net_saved > 0 else None
steps.note: Three hours saved weekly repays 24 in eight weeks.

steps.code:
manual_at_12 = 12 * manual_weekly
auto_at_12 = build_hours + 12 * auto_weekly
saved_at_12 = manual_at_12 - auto_at_12
steps.note: At week 12 total effort is 60 versus 48 hours.

walkthrough.limit: Executed Python decision arithmetic. Inputs are estimates, not measured outcomes.

visual_explanation: The cumulative-effort chart starts manual work at 0 hours and automation at its 24-hour build cost. Line slope is weekly work: 5 manual hours versus 2 ongoing automated hours at the default. The lines cross at week 8 and 40 hours; the vertical gap after the crossing is saved work. At 5 requests and 1 upkeep hour the slopes are equal, so the lines never meet. The live chart recalculates line slopes, crossing, and axis scale from the controls; its 12-week window is explicit.

title: Agent reliability: one success is not repeatable success
goal: Read repeated-trial evaluations without hiding failures behind the best attempt.
concept:
A driver reaches your house once in three attempts. That proves the route is possible. It does not prove tomorrow’s delivery will work. Agents also vary across attempts.

Look across one task’s row before counting tasks. “Any” asks whether that row contains a success. “All” asks whether it contains a failure. One failure knocks the task out of the all-success count, even when two attempts succeeded.

Across many tasks, summarize the fraction that succeeded at least once in k attempts (pass@k) or in every attempt (pass^k). The second asks for consistency. Do not present the first as if it answered the second.
example:
Our four synthetic tasks each have three clean trials: A = PPF, B = PFP, C = PPP, D = FFF. Three pass at least once: an observed 3/4 = 75%. Only C passes every trial: 1/4 = 25%. Individual trials have 7 passes out of 12. Those denominators answer different questions.

Reset files, database fixtures, and tool state before each trial. Otherwise a previous attempt may leave the answer behind or exhaust a resource. The harness must preserve comparability, not merely call the model again.

use_case.when: An agent passes a demo but users see intermittent failures, or a model change needs a reliability comparison.
use_case.example: Run a pipeline-repair agent repeatedly on isolated incident fixtures. Grade the resulting pipeline, then report consistency and failure categories for each task.
use_case.decision: At-least-once success suits cases where a human can select a verified solution. For unattended work, inspect repeatability and side effects. Neither a tiny dataset nor its average proves production safety.

practice: First read across Task A, then down the two result columns. Predict what happens if its failed third trial becomes a pass. Click “Change A’s third trial,” and watch which count moves. Then choose the repaired fixture: why can all-success rise while any-success stays at 75%?
boundary: JavaScript counts fixed synthetic outcomes; it calls no model and predicts no production probability. These observed fractions use one k-trial group per task, not the combinatorial pass@k estimator for sampling k attempts from a larger n.
sim: Blue task blocks count toward a score; empty blocks still belong to its denominator. Pass/fail labels carry the meaning as well as color.
questions: For PPF, PFP, PPP, FFF, how many tasks pass every trial?
Only PPP meets every-trial success. Three have at least one success.
After A and B become PPP, what changes?
D still fails. Removing intermittent failures improves consistency.
To prevent leftovers changing the task
Isolation removes contamination; it cannot guarantee independence or success.
written_questions: Which measure matters for an unattended repair agent, and what failures would you inspect?
Why is 75% on four tasks not a forecast for every real incident?
sources: Anthropic: demystifying evals for AI agents

steps.note: Each row is one task with three trial outcomes.

steps.code:
any_pass = [any(row) for row in trials]
all_pass = [all(row) for row in trials]
steps.note: Keep the failures while classifying tasks two ways.

steps.code:
observed_any = sum(any_pass) / len(trials)
observed_all = sum(all_pass) / len(trials)
steps.note: The same data yields 75% and 25%.

steps.code:
individual_passes = sum(sum(row) for row in trials)
trial_count = sum(len(row) for row in trials)
steps.note: Seven of twelve individual trials pass: a different denominator.

walkthrough.limit: Executed Python aggregation of synthetic results, not an agent benchmark or statistical confidence estimate.

visual_explanation: The visual reads each task horizontally, converting its three pass/fail cells into two answers: Any and All. Then it counts those answers vertically, displaying four labeled task blocks for each denominator. In the mixed fixture, A/B/C count for Any; only C counts for All. Changing A’s third cell from Fail to Pass leaves Any at 3/4 and increases All to 2/4. The separate 7/12 trial total counts cells instead of task rows. This makes the denominator difference and the hidden intermittent failures visible.

title: Flow batteries: charge returned is not energy returned
goal: Read a new battery result by separating charge efficiency from useful energy.
concept:
Returning almost every bucket of water does not mean returning the same useful energy if the water comes back at a lower height. A battery can return nearly all the charge but less energy.

Charge is measured here in ampere-hours (Ah). Energy in watt-hours (Wh) depends on charge and voltage. Coulombic efficiency compares charge out with charge in. Energy efficiency compares energy out with energy in.

A September 30 Nature Communications paper reports an alkaline iron-chromium flow cell using a ligand: a molecule that binds metal ions and changes their chemical behavior. The authors report 99.0% coulombic efficiency but 75.8% energy efficiency at 100 mA/cm² and 80% state of charge, with stability over 500 cycles. These efficiencies answer different questions.
example:
Our numbers are invented for teaching, not a reconstruction of that experiment. Put in 10 Ah at an average 1.4 V. Get back 9.9 Ah at an average 1.1 V. Charge efficiency is 99%. Energy efficiency is 10.89/14 ≈ 77.8%. The remaining 3.11 Wh is not useful output.

The paper changes metal chemistry to improve reaction behavior. It is a laboratory result, not evidence that a whole storage plant delivers the same efficiency or cost.

use_case.when: You compare emerging storage claims for long-duration supply or need to understand an efficiency headline.
use_case.example: For a possible data-center storage study, ask whether the number describes charge, cell energy, or the whole system including pumps and power conversion. This paper is a research lead, not a deployment recommendation.
use_case.decision: Compare the same measurement boundaries. Procurement would also need system-level duty-cycle, durability, safety, serviceability, and full-cost evidence. A cell result alone is insufficient.

practice: Predict which bars change when you lower discharge voltage from 1.1 to 0.7 V. Charge stays 9.9 Ah; useful energy shrinks. Then add 2 Wh of auxiliary input: does cell efficiency change, or only the system denominator?
boundary: JavaScript executes a constant-average-voltage ledger with synthetic inputs. Auxiliary consumption is extra input energy per cycle. This is not electrochemistry, a reconstruction of the paper, or a validated plant estimate. Real voltage varies over a cycle.
questions: 10 Ah in, 9.9 Ah out: what does 99% describe?
Ah measures charge; energy also depends on voltage and measurement boundary.
Why is our energy efficiency about 77.8%?
Discharge voltage is lower than charge voltage
10.89 Wh comes out after 14 Wh goes in.
Do 500 reported cell cycles prove data-center readiness?
No; system and duty-cycle evidence is still needed
A cell experiment does not validate a whole plant’s losses, durability, safety, or cost.
written_questions: What measurement boundary must match before comparing two efficiency claims?
Which numbers came from the paper and which are synthetic?
sources: Yang and colleagues: ligand engineering enables an alkaline iron-chromium redox flow battery
Published 2026-09-30; accepted 2026-09-03; early accepted manuscript; publisher abstract verified
US Department of Energy: DOE Explains… Batteries
Foundational page; publication date not displayed in retrieved page

steps.note: Set invented cycle measurements, not the paper’s raw data.

steps.code:
energy_in_wh = charge_in_ah * voltage_in
energy_out_wh = charge_out_ah * voltage_out
steps.note: 14 Wh enters; 10.89 Wh returns.

steps.code:
charge_efficiency = charge_out_ah / charge_in_ah
energy_efficiency = energy_out_wh / energy_in_wh
steps.note: Compute different quantities with different denominators.
3.11 Wh is outside useful output.

walkthrough.limit: Executed Python arithmetic, not chemistry. Average voltages stand in for integrating voltage and current over time.

visual_explanation: Two separate ledgers prevent confusing charge with energy. The charge bars compare 10 Ah in with 9.9 Ah out and remain fixed as voltage changes. The energy bar partitions total input into useful output, cell input not returned, and extra auxiliary input, all on one fixed 0–18 Wh scale. Lower discharge voltage shortens useful output and enlarges the cell-loss segment. Extra auxiliary input extends the total bar without changing useful output or the cell score: system efficiency has the larger denominator. All values in this diagram are synthetic, not measurements from the paper.

title: Deployment concurrency: one pending run or a queue?
goal: Choose whether a newer deployment replaces a waiting one or preserves it.
concept:
A building has one loading bay. One truck unloads; others wait. Two rules matter: how many trucks can unload together, and what happens to trucks already waiting when another arrives.

A GitHub Actions concurrency group permits one running job or workflow at a time. By default it keeps one pending run. A newer arrival replaces the pending run. cancel-in-progress: false protects the running job, but does not keep every waiting job.

queue: max can keep up to 100 pending jobs or runs. Combining it with cancel-in-progress: true is invalid.
example:
R1 is deploying. R2 starts waiting, then R3. By default R2 is canceled and R3 remains. With queue: max, both wait. Current ordering is FIFO by when runs start waiting on the group, not commit or dispatch order.

concurrency:
  group: production-deploy
  cancel-in-progress: false
  queue: max

This YAML fragment is not executed by this page. The Python replay executes queue bookkeeping.

use_case.when: Two workflows modify one deployment target, and overlapping changes would conflict.
use_case.example: Use the same production group for workflows in one repository sharing a target. Preserve every operation only when each must run; a latest-version deployment might deliberately replace stale pending versions.
use_case.decision: Choose by operation semantics. Required migrations still need sequence checks and queue-overflow monitoring. The group is not a cross-repository lock or a rollback mechanism.

practice: Both lanes receive the same arrival. Click “Next arrival” once: R2 waits. Before the second click, predict which lane will keep R2. Click again and point to where R2 went in each lane. Then finish R1: why do different jobs enter the deployment target?
boundary: JavaScript models one group with three runs and fixed waiting-arrival order. It makes no GitHub calls and omits runner availability, approvals, the 100-item cap, and deployment side effects. Cancellation cannot undo work already applied.
sim:
Same events, two policies. Each panel is a separate hypothetical deployment target. Only one run can occupy its green running area.

Changing this selection resets both lanes for a fresh comparison.
questions: R1 runs; R2 then R3 wait with default queue and cancel-in-progress:false. What happens?
False protects the running job, not the default pending slot.
Which setting preserves R2 and R3?
True with max is invalid. Unique groups remove mutual exclusion.
No; order uses when runs begin waiting on the group
Different preparation times can change waiting order. Sequence checks can still matter.
written_questions: When is keeping only the latest pending deployment appropriate?
How would you stop a migration running before its prerequisite?
sources: Living documentation; queue values and ordering verified

steps.note: R1 holds the shared deployment target.
R2 waits under both policies.
R3 replaces R2 only in the single-pending queue.
When R1 finishes, R3 goes next in one policy; R2 in the other.

walkthrough.limit: Executed Python bookkeeping, not a GitHub workflow. No external deployment effects.

visual_explanation: Two stacked queue diagrams receive the same arrival and completion events. Each separates a single running deployment target, the pending area, a canceled tray, and completed runs. After R2 then R3 arrive, the default lane moves R2 to the canceled tray and retains R3. The max lane retains R2 then R3. Finishing R1 visibly moves R3 into one target and R2 into the other. The distinction is pending-job retention, not a change to the one-running-job limit. Panels compare hypothetical policies; they are not two live deployment groups.

title: Keyset pagination: continue after a row, not a position
goal: Keep the next API page stable when earlier rows are inserted.
tag: Foundation · API design and SQL ordering
concept:
You bookmark a book with “after the paragraph about B.” Someone inserts a page near the front. Your paragraph bookmark still works; “skip two paragraphs” lands somewhere else.

Offset pagination counts positions. Keyset pagination remembers the last row’s ordering values and asks for rows after them. Use a unique order: here (created_at, id). The ID breaks ties between equal timestamps.
example:
Start with A,B,C,D. Page 1 returns A,B. Insert X before them. Skipping two rows now repeats B. Seeking after (10,B) returns C,D.

SELECT created_at, id FROM events
WHERE (created_at, id) > (:last_time, :last_id)
ORDER BY created_at, id
LIMIT 2;

For this non-null ascending order, a matching composite index supports the seek. The SQL is a reference snippet; the Python replay executes equivalent tuple comparisons on a list.

use_case.when: A list API has many pages or frequent inserts, and clients mostly move forward through sorted results.
use_case.example: An event-catalog endpoint returns records after its last (ingested_at, event_id) cursor. Bind cursors to tenant, filters, and ordering, and validate them before querying.
use_case.decision: Choose keyset for forward traversal with a suitable index. Offset is simpler for small static lists and page-number navigation. A consistent full export may also need a snapshot or cutoff: a cursor alone is not a snapshot.

practice: Compare each row’s old and new position. Find B: why does OFFSET return it twice after X arrives? Then switch to a one-row first page and locate the row skipped by a timestamp-only cursor.
boundary: JavaScript filters synthetic tuples; it does not execute SQL or sign cursors. Rows inserted behind the cursor can be missed. Changes to sort keys, deletion, null ordering, direction, and collation need explicit treatment in a real API.
questions: After page A,B and insertion of X before A, what does OFFSET 2 return?
Positions shift. B becomes third and is returned again.
After a one-row page ends at A with time 10, why include ID?
B shares that time and must not be skipped
Seeking strictly after time 10 skips B. Tuple (10,B) follows (10,A).
Will keyset include every later row inserted behind its cursor?
No; it is not a snapshot or change stream
A seek returns rows beyond the current boundary. Complete export is a separate requirement.
written_questions: Which index and cursor fields suit a tenant-scoped event API?
How does a consistent export requirement change your design?

steps.note: The last row becomes bookmark (10,B).
X changes positions, not bookmark values.
Skipping two repeats B.

steps.code: keyset_page2 = [row for row in rows if row > cursor][:2]
steps.note: Seeking after (10,B) returns C,D.

walkthrough.limit: Executed Python list example, not PostgreSQL. Non-null values, ascending order, simple A–D IDs.

visual_explanation: The row table keeps each event’s identity visible while showing its old and new position. Inserting X changes B from position 2 to position 3. OFFSET 2 skips positions 1 and 2, so it returns B again. The cursor line stays after the same tuple (10,B), so seeking returns C,D. With a one-row first page, (10,B) is after (10,A), although its timestamp is equal: a time-only test incorrectly skips B.
